rows.evidence: Q1: Conditions and Methodology / Results <U+2013> author's own 2007 season data from 10 Watermark sensor nodes at 12 and 24 in. and 43 pressure-chamber leaf water potential points on a 4.4-acre clay-soil Cabernet vineyard. Q2: Vineyard section and Results <U+2013> 2007 yield 3.97 t/acre (record, up from 1.81) and Brix peaking at 26.5<U+2013>28 under soil-tension-guided modified RDI; Results state the season's success in yield, ripeness and reduced water use supports the modified RDI approach, though indirectly; Fig. 3 shows 24-in. tension correlates with leaf water potential (R2 0.42). Q4: Results/Fig. 3 <U+2013> the intermediate vine water stress (midday leaf water potential by pressure chamber) was measured and related to the 24-in. soil tension used to set irrigation targets. Q6: Vineyard/Results <U+2013> yield and management outcomes reported for the whole commercial 4.4-acre vineyard managed as several irrigation blocks (farm level). Q7: Abstract/Results <U+2013> effect obtained only when sampled sufficiently (2<U+2013>3 sites/acre) and at appropriate depth; 24-in. tension correlated, 12-in. did not; minimum 2-h irrigation duration set because of line-pressure transients. Q8: Results <U+2013> authors state support for the approach is indirect because many confounding factors affect yield; outliers from location 505 removed, raising R2 from 0.26 to 0.42; values beyond <U+2013>300 cB discarded as open connections.
rows.notes: Crop-production evidence is observational: one vineyard, one season, no control treatment; the yield increase coincides with the second year of production of young vines, which the author acknowledges as confounded. The review's details (150 kPa criterion at 60 cm, stem water potential) do not appear in this text; the study uses a <U+2013>13 bar leaf water potential threshold and reports an R2, not a dispersion measure (Q9 no). Q6 given as yes on the basis of farm-level reporting, with doubt since the farm is a single 4.4-acre vineyard.

rows.evidence: Q1: Conditions and Methodology <U+2013> author's own soil tension network data and pressure-chamber measurements from the 2007 season. Q2: Irrigation Paradigm <U+2013> 2007 irrigation totalled 34 gal/vine, a 26% reduction from 46 gal/vine in 2006, under the soil-tension-based modified RDI; Results <U+2013> irrigation was delayed in 2007 until a higher stress level and durations/intervals were set from the 24-in. tension data and forecast water use; the season's success in reduced water use is said to support the approach. Q4: Results <U+2013> intermediate variables measured: average soil tension at 24 in. maintained at a target, irrigation interval/duration adjusted from wetting-front delay between 12 and 24 in., and leaf water potential spot-checked to verify stress did not exceed threshold. Q6: Irrigation Paradigm <U+2013> water use per vine reported for the whole vineyard (farm) managed in irrigation blocks. Q7: Abstract/Results <U+2013> sensors must be at an appropriate depth (24 in., not 12 in.) and sampled at sufficient density (2<U+2013>3 sites/acre); minimum 2-h duration required for uniform application. Q8: Results <U+2013> authors state the support from yield, ripeness and reduced water use is indirect because of many confounding factors.
rows.notes: Water savings are reported only as a year-to-year comparison (2006 vs 2007) with no control; 2007 was a very dry year with water trucked in and intervals lengthened to match available supply, so savings are confounded with water scarcity. No dispersion measure is given for water use (Q9 no). The review's 150 kPa / 60 cm criterion is not stated in this text. Q6 yes with doubt (single 4.4-acre vineyard treated as farm level).

notes: Full text appears complete (conference-style paper, figures described). The study's principal result is a correlation between Watermark soil tension at 24 in. and midday leaf water potential (R2 0.42, n=43) on one clay-soil vineyard in one season; yield and water-use outcomes are reported as uncontrolled observations the author himself calls indirect and confounded.
